claims.says: Jul-Sep
Roughly late June through September

contradictions.why: The optimal window starts in late June, before the route's own Jul-Sep season.

claims.says: typically closed by snow from mid-November into spring; reopening timing is variable year to year (historically mid-April to mid-June)
closes gate-to-gate roughly early December–mid/late April

contradictions.why: Two fields give different closing (mid-November vs early December) and reopening windows for the same highway.

claims.says: No climbing permit required; free self-issued wilderness permit for overnight
No climbing or overnight permit required
outside any designated wilderness — no quota, no reservation and no self-issue permit

contradictions.why: The raw access record still says an overnight self-issue wilderness permit is needed while the rendered access and bivy fields say none and that the area is outside wilderness.
contradictions.internal_resolution: access.permit, access.overnight_permit and both bivy entries agree there is no permit; the _raw value is the outlier.

claims.says: Descent

contradictions.why: PUBLISHED TIMES labels the whole 11-hour second day (camp to summit to car) as descent time, while the schedule has 7 hours from the summit to the trailhead.
contradictions.internal_resolution: The itinerary schedule is internally consistent: 4:30 AM from camp, summit 9:00 AM, car 4:00 PM. The 11 h is the whole of day 2, not the descent, and the sectionBreakdown labels (Climb for the approach, Descent for day 2) are swapped.

contradictions.fact: Gain and distance to the Bench camp on day 1

claims.says: Reach the Bench camp below Burgundy Col

contradictions.why: Day 1 gains 4,400 ft over 3.3 mi to reach a camp that the row puts at 6,460 ft and 2.3 mi from a 4,300 ft trailhead, about 2,400 ft of gain. The day-1 figures fit Burgundy Col (7,800 ft, 3 mi) instead.
contradictions.internal_resolution: The waypoints, approach ("~6,460 ft") and bivy (6450) agree on the Bench, so the day-1 gain and miles are the outlier. This may overlap the settled "Total gain" item.

contradictions.fact: Objective named in the partner and hazard fields

claims.says: carrying a rock rack, rope, and rappel gear to the base of the Wine Spires
exposed 5th-class pitches on the Wine Spires towers
Every Wine Spires objective ... is reached by going to Burgundy Col and then SOUTH or EAST from it. Ares Tower is the one you reach by contouring and scrambling NORTH

contradictions.why: The partner and hazard fields describe the Wine Spires as the destination, but the route is Ares Tower, and the approach tells climbers that the Wine Spires lie in the opposite direction.
contradictions.internal_resolution: The approach, baseFinding, beta and waypoints all describe Ares Tower north of the col, so the text naming the Wine Spires was carried over from a neighbouring route.

claims.says: typically mid-April to about mid-November
typically mid-April to ~mid-November
closes gate-to-gate roughly early December–mid/late April

contradictions.why: The highway is said to close in mid-November in two fields and in early December in another.

claims.says: Nuts and cams to about 4 in
cams (0.5 to 3 size range)
single rack 0.3-3in
Cams 0.5-3in

contradictions.why: The gear list says cams to 4 inches while every rack field stops at 3 inches.
contradictions.internal_resolution: Three rack fields agree on a rack to 3 inches, so gear[0] is the outlier.

contradictions.fact: Descent time from the summit to the car

claims.says: approach roughly 3-4 hours each way

contradictions.why: The itinerary gives the hike 3-4 hours each way, but PUBLISHED TIMES allows 2 hours for the whole descent, including the North Ridge scramble.

claims.says: good camping and a late-season spring are near 6,400-6,500 ft
the late-season spring near the bench camp may be the only water
limited to non-existent by late summer and early autumn

contradictions.why: The approach and the September guidance count on a late-season spring at the Bench camp, but the camp card says water there is limited to non-existent by late summer.

claims.says: fairly sustained 5.10a/b climbing
The second-hardest pitch: a strenuous 5.10b finger-crack layback

contradictions.why: The crux pitch in ROUTE BREAKDOWN is graded 5.10d, but the header and the prose top out at 5.10b. The P4 notes themselves describe 5.8+ to 5.9+ chimney and offwidth moves.
contradictions.internal_resolution: The rock_grade, beta, waypoint note ("5.10a/b") and P8 being the "second-hardest" at 5.10b all agree. The 5.10d on P4 is the outlier.

contradictions.fact: Net gain from the trailhead to Snowy Lakes camp

claims.says: about 2,800-3,000 ft of net elevation gain from the trailhead to camp

contradictions.why: The approach puts net gain to camp at 2,800-3,000 ft, but the row's own trailhead (4,880 ft) and camp (6,700 ft) give about 1,820 ft net, which matches the itinerary's 2,300 gain less 400 loss.
contradictions.internal_resolution: The waypoints and itinerary day 1 agree on about 1,900 ft net. The 2,800-3,000 ft figure matches the height of the gully base (7,800 ft), not camp.

contradictions.fact: Which Snowy Lake to camp at

claims.says: Lower Snowy Lake is the one to camp at for this route; Upper Snowy sits higher and farther from the peak.
Upper Snowy Lake is preferred for views; Lower Snowy Lake camps are also common

contradictions.why: The waypoint tells parties to camp at Lower Snowy Lake, while the itinerary calls Upper Snowy Lake the preferred camp.
contradictions.internal_resolution: The waypoint note, approach and baseFinding all base the route at Lower Snowy Lake.

contradictions.fact: Ridge used to reach the summit

claims.says: looking for the easiest place to gain the south ridge
Once on the south ridge crest
descend by reversing the gully and cave-ledge system back to the west-ridge notch

contradictions.why: ROUTE BREAKDOWN reaches the summit by the south ridge, but the summit waypoint sends the descent back to a west-ridge notch.

claims.says: Jul–Sep
Mid-July, once the summit gully has largely melted out, through early-to-mid October. Late September into early October is prime
Mid-July through mid-September

contradictions.why: best_season runs into mid-October and calls early October prime, which is outside both the Jul–Sep season and the optimal window.

claims.says: Break down tent and reload overnight pack.

contradictions.why: Day 2 shows a pack weight of 0 lb, but it includes carrying the full overnight pack out from Snowy Lakes.
contradictions.internal_resolution: Day 1 lists a 35 lb overnight pack, and the same pack is carried out on day 2.

contradictions.fact: Which trailhead the plan starts from

claims.says: Rainy Pass PCT North Trailhead
Rainy Pass Trailhead (PCT North parking lot, SR-20)
Park at the unmarked pullout on SR-20 about 3.1 miles east of Rainy Pass (~5,000 ft)
Meadow rising traverse
Boot path tops out on the level section of Whistler's south ridge here

contradictions.why: The TRAILHEAD card and the only Trailhead waypoint are the Rainy Pass PCT lot (Option A). The itinerary, timing and the waypoint chain (meadow 0.5 mi, south-ridge gain 0.9 mi) are Option B from the unmarked pullout 3.1 mi east, which has no waypoint.

contradictions.fact: Direction of the Option B traverse to the south ridge

claims.says: THEN RISING-TRAVERSE EAST TO INTERSECT THE LEVEL PORTION OF WHISTLER'S SOUTH RIDGE AT ABOUT 6,180 FT

contradictions.why: The prose says to traverse east from a pullout that lies east of the peak. The row's own meadow and ridge-gain waypoints step west toward the summit.

claims.says: three pitches of the Great Chimney lead to the top
Two short technical pitches (5.3 entry, 5.4 exit past a large chockstone

contradictions.why: The beta says two technical pitches, while the pitches column, ROUTE BREAKDOWN and the summit waypoint give three.
contradictions.internal_resolution: Three fields agree on three pitches. The beta is the outlier.

contradictions.fact: Distance and gain to High Pass

claims.says: High Pass itself (~5,960 ft, roughly 2 miles and about 750 ft of gain from the trailhead)
roughly two and a half miles with a little over a thousand feet of gain

contradictions.why: The High Pass camp card gives 2.5 mi and over 1,000 ft of gain to the pass. The approach, variant and waypoint give 2 mi and 750 ft, which matches 5,200 to 5,960 ft.
contradictions.internal_resolution: The approach, approach_variants, waypoints and the elevations all agree on 2 mi and 750 ft.

claims.says: Watson Lakes Trailhead
Drive Baker Lake Road (FR-11) to FR-1106, then FR-1107 to its end at the Watson Lakes Trailhead (~4,360 ft
From the Bacon Creek Road trailhead (~800 ft), follow the old, downed-tree-choked roadbed for about 2.5 miles
Return to Bacon Creek Road
back over the Mt. Watson sidehill, saddle, and Anderson Lakes ridge path to the Watson Lakes Trailhead
planned from the Bacon Creek Road trailhead (~800 ft) on the south side, not the Watson Lakes trailhead used in the approach

contradictions.why: The TRAILHEAD card, approach, waypoints and DESCENT use the Watson Lakes trailhead (about 4,300 ft). The itinerary, timing and the gain_ft/dist_km columns use the Bacon Creek Road trailhead (about 800 ft) by the southeast ridge and Peak 4800. The page describes two different trips as one.
contradictions.internal_resolution: road.driveNote says FR-1107 to the Watson Lakes trailhead is closed by a washout and Bacon Creek Road is the only drivable approach, but the approach, waypoints and descent were not updated to match.

claims.says: all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center)
No wilderness permit required for camps within the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness (national forest) portion
No overnight permit required on the national forest side; camp only in designated sites at Watson Lakes
This basin lies on the North Cascades National Park side of the divide, so a park backcountry permit for the correct cross-country zone is required

contradictions.why: The permit field says every overnight stay needs a park permit, while the access fields say forest-side camps need none. The Upper Diobsud Lakes card puts the standard lakes camp on the park side, requiring a permit.

contradictions.fact: Location and height of the Diobsud Lakes camp

claims.says: Diobsud basin
in the upper Diobsud Creek basin on the far side of Bacon Peak from the Anderson Creek road
descending through heather to the Diobsud Lakes basin ... the last dependable camp/water source below the peak

contradictions.why: The approach camps in the Diobsud Lakes basin between Mt. Watson and Bacon, at about 4,900 ft on the waypoint. The camp card puts Upper Diobsud Lakes at 6,000 ft on the far side of Bacon from the Watson road.

claims.says: climbs about 0.5 mile to a ridge saddle (~1.4-1.5 miles and ~600 ft above the trailhead)
Continue roughly another mile ... to a second junction at ~4,700 ft
Trail forks here — right drops 0.5mi to Lower Anderson Lake
over a saddle at around 4,700 ft

contradictions.why: The approach places the saddle half a mile past a junction that is already about 2 miles in, yet calls the saddle 1.4-1.5 mi from the trailhead. It is also about 600 ft above the trailhead (about 4,960 ft), while the waypoint and Watson Lakes card merge junction and saddle at 4,700 ft.

claims.says: FR-1107 (Anderson-Watson Road) has been closed at Mile Post 3.8 by a washout since July 8, 2026
an atmospheric river in December 2025 cut a washout in FS 1107 at around mile three to four

contradictions.why: The road note dates the closure to July 8, 2026, while the trailhead card attributes it to a December 2025 washout that already closed the trailhead.

claims.says: Reach the ~6,250-6,300 ft saddle camp on the Diobsud Creek Glacier
Cross the Diobsud Creek Glacier heading northwest, probing for crevasses.
Gain the south ridge
Broad snow slopes on the south ridge lead onto the toe of the Diobsud Creek Glacier ... head northwest toward the saddle below the summit
Saddle at 6,250 ft to the summit

contradictions.why: The summit-day schedule leaves a camp at the 6,250 ft saddle, crosses the glacier, then gains the south ridge. CLIMBING ROUTE runs south ridge, then glacier, then saddle, then summit, so the ridge sits below the camp.

routes.name: Last Chance for Gas, AKA Tricky Start

contradictions.fact: Gain from the river to the Cinderella-Little Sister notch

claims.says: Elevation gain from the river crossing to this notch is substantial — on the order of 4,500-5,500 ft over several miles
Little Sister saddle

contradictions.why: The approach puts 4,500-5,500 ft of gain between the river and the notch, but the row puts the river at about 2,000 ft and the notch at 5,800 ft, about 3,800 ft. Its figure would place the notch above the 6,431 ft summit.
contradictions.internal_resolution: The waypoints and the total gain (5,400 ft to a 6,431 ft summit) fit a notch near 5,800 ft. The approach range is the outlier.

contradictions.fact: Car-to-car distance with the road closure

claims.says: ~12 miles and ~5,400 ft of gain
FS Road 38 is closed by a washout at milepost 7, about 4 miles short of the trailhead

contradictions.why: The walk alone is 12 mi round trip (summit 6 mi from the trailhead), yet the day is called "~12 miles" car-to-car while also biking 4 closed road miles each way, about 20 mi in total.

marginal

spring avalanche hazard off the nearby 'Mythic Wall' for parties descending on snow

claims.says: Free self-issue Mount Baker Wilderness permit or trailhead registration
self-issue Mt. Baker Wilderness permit at the kiosk
A free self-issued wilderness permit is available at the trailhead register for day use
No climbing or wilderness permit.

claims.says: V-thread hardware for descent
V-thread hardware for descent
There is no rappelling on the standard descent.
None required — walk-off descent via the Coleman-Deming route

claims.says: Reach Hogsback / Coleman-Deming bench (~6,600 ft)
Camp sites scattered 6,000-6,200 ft along the moraine crest

contradictions.why: The schedule puts the Hogsback at about 6,600 ft, while the waypoint puts it at 6,000-6,200 ft.
contradictions.internal_resolution: The waypoint and the Polish Route row agree on 6,000-6,200 ft.

claims.says: A descent mixing short V-thread rappels with downclimbing, on threads you build yourself
From the summit, walk off ... V-thread rappels are for retreating from partway up, not the normal way down.
No rappel descent is on record.

contradictions.why: An approach hazard describes the descent as V-thread rappels mixed with downclimbing, while descent, descent_text and rappels all say it is a walk-off.
contradictions.internal_resolution: descent, descent_text, rappels and gear[4] agree on a walk-off. The variant hazard is the outlier.

contradictions.fact: Which pitch is the WI6 crux

claims.says: Pitch 2 (crux): Steep ice for approximately 30 feet, easing briefly, then rising to a free-hanging ice dagger grading WI6.
WI4
true

60 m rope

contradictions.why: The gear list calls for two ropes, but the detailed rack, which takes precedence in PROTECTION + RACK, lists one 60 m rope. That limits V-thread retreat rappels to 30 m.

claims.says: N

The face is northwest-facing
this northwest-facing finish

claims.says: roughly 12-13 hrs round trip
with an ~11-hour car-to-car day

contradictions.fact: Height of the East Peak above the West Peak

claims.says: ~120 ft higher than the West Peak across the basin
easy to mistake the 6,600 ft false (west) summit for the true 6,891 ft east summit
false (west, ~6,600 ft) and true (east, 6,891 ft) summits

contradictions.why: The summit waypoint says the East Peak is about 120 ft higher than the West Peak, while the rest of the row puts the West Peak at about 6,600 ft, about 290 ft lower. The waypoint was not updated when the West Peak height was fixed.
contradictions.internal_resolution: The overview, hazards, watch_out, approach, climbing_route and baseFinding all use about 6,600 ft for the West Peak.

claims.says: exposure is generally minimal for experienced parties
a short Class 3 step near the top has real exposure
hard class 3 scrambling to the small, exposed summit

contradictions.why: The beta calls the exposure minimal, while the watch-out and ROUTE BREAKDOWN describe real exposure at the summit step.

claims.says: Cougar Divide comes in from the NORTH-WEST via Dobbs Creek; Skyline Divide comes in from the WEST
the connection east along the ridge leads to Hadley
continue cross-country south along the open ridge

contradictions.why: The baseFinding says Cougar Divide approaches from the northwest, but the row's own trailhead lies northeast of the summit. The camp card sends parties east to Hadley, while the approach says south, and the summit is actually southwest.

claims.says: Open ridge with no shelter and no water beyond the trailhead
A creek fed by a lingering snowfield runs at the upper camp through most of the season, and there are ponds along the divide

contradictions.why: An approach hazard says there is no water past the trailhead, while the meadow camp card describes a creek and ponds along the divide.
